title: A battery is a bucket of pushes
interaction: Put a battery in a torch, switch it on and let the clock run: a gauge shows the store draining and the beam dimming over hours. Fit a bigger bulb and the store empties faster; add a second battery end to end and the bulb is brighter but the pair runs down sooner; put the two side by side and the bulb is as before but lasts twice as long. A counter records the hours each arrangement gives.
takeaway: A battery holds a fixed store, so a brighter lamp means a shorter life, and two batteries can be stacked for more push or paired for more hours.
pitfall: A battery does not store electricity or electrons: it stores a chemical push, and the electrons that flow were in the wire all along. The bulb does not use current up: the same current leaves the battery as returns to it, and what the bulb takes is the store.

title: Bicycle gears
interaction: Turn the pedals one full turn and count how many times the back wheel turns with the chain on each pair of sprockets. Then set a hill and pedal: a gauge shows how hard each push must be and a marker shows how far one push carries the bike. Shift while climbing to find the gear that is light enough to push and still gets you up.
takeaway: A small sprocket in front and a big one at the back turn the wheel less per pedal turn, so each push is easier but carries you a shorter way; no gear gives you more for free.
pitfall: A low gear does not make the rider stronger or add energy: it trades distance for force, and the wheel turns less for every pedal turn.

title: Bicycle gears: why low gear gets you up the hill
interaction: Pedal a bicycle along a road that rises into a hill and shift gears: in a high gear each pedal turn carries you far but the pedals go stiff on the slope and you grind to a halt; in a low gear the pedals spin easily and the bike climbs, slower. Counters show wheel turns per pedal turn and the push needed on the pedal, and a rider of the same strength tries each gear on the same hill.
takeaway: Gears trade distance for push: a low gear turns the wheel less per pedal stroke but needs less force, which is what gets a rider up a hill.
pitfall: A low gear gives no extra energy and makes no hill shorter: you pedal more turns for the same climb. Gears do not make a bike faster on their own; at the same effort a high gear is faster only where the road is flat.

title: Car brakes
interaction: Press the brake pedal and follow the push: the pedal is a lever, the small piston it moves squeezes fluid that cannot be squashed into the big pistons at the wheels, and those press the pads onto the spinning discs, with gauges showing the force and the distance moved at each stage. Then drive at a chosen speed and brake: the discs glow with the car's motion turned into heat, and the stopping distance grows four times when the speed doubles; wet the road and the tyres skid before the brakes run out.
takeaway: A light push on the pedal becomes a crushing squeeze at the wheels because fluid passes the push on to bigger pistons, the car's motion ends up as heat in the discs, and twice the speed needs four times the distance.
pitfall: Brake fluid does not squash to absorb the push, and the brakes do not stop the car: they stop the wheels, and it is the tyres gripping the road that stops the car.

title: Click pen
interaction: Press the button of a retractable pen and step through what happens inside: the plunger's slanted teeth push the cam down and twist it part of a turn, the spring pushes it back up, and the cam lands either on a tooth, which holds the tip out, or slides into a slot, which lets it back in. Scrub the clicks back and forth with the barrel made transparent and count how many it takes for the cam to come round to where it started; then press the tip to paper and watch the ball roll a film of ink out of the tube.
takeaway: Every click turns the cam one notch, so it lands alternately on a tooth and in a slot, which is why one press puts the tip out and the next brings it back.
pitfall: The pen has no switch that remembers: its memory is the cam's angle, and the ball does not squirt ink, it rolls it out like a tiny paint roller.

title: Pendulum clocks & the escapement
interaction: Hang a weight on a cord that turns a toothed wheel and watch the wheel spin away in a blur; add the anchor that rocks with a pendulum, and the wheel can now advance only one tooth per swing, with a tick each time a tooth is caught and a tiny push back to the pendulum to keep it going. takeaway: The weight drives the clock and the pendulum only meters it out, one tooth per swing, so the length of the pendulum sets the time and a heavier weight hardly changes the rate.
pitfall: The pendulum does not power the clock, and a bigger swing does not tick faster: for small swings the length alone sets the period.

title: Tower cranes: why they don't fall over

title: Dams and water wheels: the push is in the height

title: The differential: how a car turns a corner
interaction: Drive a toy car round a bend and watch the outer wheel roll farther than the inner one; lock the two wheels to one axle and the inner tyre skids. Open the axle to show the differential: a ring gear turns a cage, and two small gears inside let one wheel turn faster while the other turns slower by exactly as much, a turn counter on each wheel adding up to twice the cage's. Drag the bend tighter and the counters split further; put one wheel on ice and watch it spin while the other stops.
takeaway: A differential lets two driven wheels turn at different speeds while one shaft drives both, which is what turning a corner without skidding needs.
pitfall: The differential does not send more torque to the outer wheel: it gives both wheels the same torque, which is why one wheel on ice spins and the other stops (the problem a limited-slip differential addresses).

title: How a drone steers with four rotors
interaction: Four speed dials, one per rotor, with each rotor's push drawn as an arrow on the drone. title: Elevator
interaction: Put people into the cab one at a time and watch the rope over the wheel at the top: a counterweight on the other side balances the empty cab plus about half a load, so the motor only lifts the difference, shown on a gauge that is lowest with the cab half full and highest going up full or down empty. title: Escalator
interaction: Scrub the chain of an escalator and follow one step round the loop: it rides on two pairs of wheels on two separate tracks, and because the tracks sit one step-height apart on the slope and level out at the ends, the step stays flat all the way up, sinks into a flat floor at the top and turns over underneath. title: Electric kettle

title: Why a light bulb glows (and gets hot)

title: Lock & key
interaction: Cut a key by setting the depth of each of its five notches, slide it into a pin-tumbler lock and watch each spring-loaded pin stack ride up its notch. title: Skyscrapers in the wind

title: Where the work goes: exergy
interaction: Hover over each component of a modelled coal, gas or nuclear steam plant and see a Grassmann diagram: the flow of work potential, exergy, shrinking from fuel to electricity, with the part destroyed in each component drawn as a leak. takeaway: Most of a steam plant's lost work potential is destroyed inside the boiler, where heat drops from flame temperature to steam temperature, not in the condenser where the energy is visibly thrown away.

title: Flywheel energy storage
interaction: Spin a flywheel faster with a slider and watch the stored energy grow with the square of the speed while the hoop and radial stresses, computed across the rotating disc or rim from the elasticity solution, grow with it; choose steel, aluminum or carbon-fiber composite and the rim bursts, drawn as a ring of fragments, at the speed where stress reaches the material's strength. A chart of energy per kilogram against strength over density shows why the light material wins; then let it coast with bearing friction and air drag at a chosen vacuum level and watch the self-discharge.
takeaway: A flywheel's energy per kilogram is set by its material's strength divided by its density, so the lightest rim stores the most before it bursts, and only a vacuum and good bearings keep it stored.
pitfall: Heavier is not better: for a given material a bigger mass only stores more in proportion, while energy per kilogram is fixed by strength over density.

title: Fuel cells & the hydrogen round trip

title: Geothermal power
interaction: Drill an injection and a production well into hot rock and pump water around the loop: a two-dimensional heat-transport model in the rock shows the cold front advancing from the injector over years until it breaks through at the producer and the output temperature starts to drop. Set the well spacing, the flow rate and the rock temperature, and a binary power cycle at the surface converts the heat with the low efficiency that a 150 to 200 degree source allows.

title: Transmission lines, AC and DC

Set the converter stations' losses and cost and find the break-even distance where DC wins.

title: Hydraulic machines

title: Inside a lithium-ion cell under load

interaction: Start with an actuator disc: drag how much the air slows through the rotor and watch the stream tube widen, the thrust and power change, and the power coefficient peak at 16/27. Then replace the disc with real blades: set the tip-speed ratio, the blade pitch and the twist, and a blade-element-momentum model with a measured airfoil polar computes the angle of attack along the blade, the power curve against wind speed, and the stall or pitch regulation that holds power steady above rated wind.
takeaway: No rotor can take more than 59 percent of the wind's power because the air must keep moving to get out of the way, and real blades approach that only near one tip-speed ratio.
needs: Lift and drag polars of a wind-turbine airfoil: NREL S809 wind-tunnel data or the NREL 5-MW reference turbine's airfoil tables (US government laboratory, openly published), or NACA airfoil data (public domain).
pitfall: The Betz limit is not a design shortcoming of today's turbines; it applies to any device that takes energy from a free stream, so a rotor near 50 percent is close to perfect.
why: Penn State AERSP 583 Wind Turbine Aerodynamics (actuator disc, Betz limit, blade element momentum theory): https://www.e-education.psu.edu/aersp583/ (from search results); also the OpenMDAO Betz-limit worked example https://openmdao.org/docs/latest/examples/betz_limit.html.
overlapWith: flight: it reuses the airfoil polar, but the graphic is the whole rotor and the momentum balance of the stream through it; solar-cells is the only other page with a hard physical ceiling on efficiency.
